summary: Surveys peer-to-peer systems, giving a definition and several ways to classify them. It describes which kinds of applications can be built with P2P technology and gives examples of P2P applications in use. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo tries to settle what peer-to-peer means. Its test is simple: the computers in the system must both ask for services and provide them. It then sorts the systems that pass and fail that test, and explains when the approach is worth using.

questions: what are the types of p2p systems
when should i use peer-to-peer instead of client-server
subtitle: A working definition of peer-to-peer, the ways such systems are classified, and when they pay off.

tldr.problem: Engineers designing systems have no shared understanding of what counts as peer-to-peer, and in the telecom industry the term is often taken to mean illegal file sharing.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a peer-to-peer system as one whose elements both request and provide services, then applies that definition to the DNS, SIP, P2PSIP and BitTorrent, and sets out the functions such a system must provide.
tldr.outcome: It classifies systems by how they index data and by how decentralised they are, describes four families of application, and argues that the choice between peer-to-peer and client-server has to be made case by case.

today: RFC 5694 is an Informational memo published in November 2009, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a survey and a set of guidelines rather than a specification, and it notes that the Internet Research Task Force had a research group working on peer-to-peer systems.

sections.title: Defining a Peer-to-Peer System
sections.content:
Peer-to-peer systems have received a great deal of attention, with an IRTF research group on them and several commercial and non-commercial applications running on the Internet, some of them among the most widely used applications there. Yet engineers designing systems or writing specifications do not share a common understanding of what a peer-to-peer system is, and many people in the telecom and datacom industries believe the term is synonymous with illegal activity such as unauthorised exchange of content or botnets. The goal of the document is to discuss the trade-offs in deciding whether a particular application is best designed as peer-to-peer or on a different model such as client-server, and to provide architectural guidelines for that decision. The document stresses that peer-to-peer systems can implement perfectly legitimate applications and business models.

The term is used in many contexts with slightly different meanings, and there is no clear border between a peer-to-peer paradigm and the supposedly opposite client-server one. Some architectures are clearly one or the other, while others can be considered either or both depending on the definition being used. The definition used here is that a system is peer-to-peer if the elements that form it share their resources to provide the service the system is designed to provide, and the elements both provide services to other elements and request services from other elements. In practice a system can have a few exceptions and still count, for example a centralised enrolment server. A system where most endpoints behave as clients could not be strictly peer-to-peer. Many definitions also assume that the nodes take part in transactions for services that do not directly benefit them, that the peers can talk to each other directly without passing through intermediaries, and that the system is self-organising with decentralised control.

The definition is applied to four systems. The DNS is a hierarchical distributed system that has been classified both as client-server and as peer-to-peer, but under this definition it is not peer-to-peer, because DNS resolvers are service requesters and not service providers. Traditional SIP, a rendezvous protocol that lets a user locate a remote user and establish a session, is not peer-to-peer either: user agents register with a central server for their domain and share their resources only for their own benefit, since each is involved only in transactions for sessions that involve itself. In P2PSIP, user agents register their contact information with an overlay formed by the user agents themselves rather than with a central server, and they take part in transactions that do not benefit them directly, so it is a peer-to-peer system. BitTorrent, used to distribute files, is a peer-to-peer system because endpoints download pieces from other endpoints and upload pieces to them, though a swarm where most endpoints were infrastructure nodes holding the complete file from the start would not strictly qualify, since most of them would only be providing services.
sections.plainLanguage: The test is whether the computers in the system give as well as take. A DNS resolver only takes, so the DNS fails. A BitTorrent peer both downloads and uploads, so it passes.

sections.title: The Functions of a Peer-to-Peer System
sections.content:
Peer-to-peer systems include several functions, some of which are independent of the service provided and handle how peers connect to the system. The enrolment function gives nodes joining the system the credentials they need to join, and handles node authentication and authorisation. The peer discovery function lets nodes find peers already in the system so they can connect to them. Both are provided in a centralised way in some systems, through a central enrolment server and a central peer discovery server, sometimes called a bootstrap server. Taxonomies do not take these two functions into account when classifying systems; they classify on how the remaining functions are implemented.

The remaining functions depend on the service being provided, and not every system implements all of them. A system used only for storing data may not implement the computing function, and one used only for computing may not implement data storage. The data indexing function deals with indexing the data stored in the system. The data storage function deals with storing and retrieving data from the system. The computation function deals with the computing performed by the system, which can relate to data processing or real-time media processing. The message transport function deals with message exchanges between peers; depending on how it is implemented, peers can exchange protocol messages through a central server, directly with each other, or through peers that provide overlay routing.

Providing a service typically involves processing or storing data, so in a peer-to-peer system the peers share their processing and storage capacity. For a file distribution service, different peers store different files, and a peer that wants a particular file first discovers which peers have it and then obtains it from them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every such system needs to admit new nodes, let them find each other, index and store data, do any computing, and pass messages about. Which of those are centralised and which are shared is what distinguishes one design from another.

sections.title: Ways of Classifying Peer-to-Peer Systems
sections.content:
Taxonomies classify elements into groups so that they can be studied more easily, and they give a common vocabulary. Since different authors cannot agree on one definition of peer-to-peer, it is no surprise that there are many taxonomies. Classifying systems by different traits is normal, but different authors using the same term for different things, as happens with the first and second generations of peer-to-peer systems, confuses readers.

The most useful classification is said to have to do with the way data is indexed, that is, how the data indexing function is implemented. An index can be centralised, with a central server keeping references to the data in all peers; local, with each peer keeping references only to its own data; or distributed, with references to data residing at several nodes. Napster, early versions of Gnutella up to version 0.4, and distributed hash table based systems are examples of centralised, local and distributed indexes respectively. Indexes can also be classified as semantic, able to capture relationships between documents and their metadata, or semantic-free, which cannot. Semantic indexes allow richer searches but sometimes fail to find data that is actually in the system.

Other authors classify systems by their level of decentralisation. Hybrid systems need a central entity to provide their services, while pure systems can keep providing their services when any single peer is removed. Under that definition, systems with a centralised index are hybrid, and systems with local or distributed indexes are pure. Pure systems can further be classified by how much structure they show: in unstructured systems peers join by connecting to any other peers, and in structured systems they connect to well-defined peers chosen by their logical identifiers. The border is blurry, because unstructured systems have evolved to show some structure and to use distributed indexes.

Talk of generations is said to be not useful in a technical context, because generations are defined differently by different authors and because the wording implies that later generations are better. Depending on the application, a system of an earlier generation may meet its requirements better than one of a later generation.
sections.plainLanguage: The most useful way to sort these systems is by where the index lives: in one central server, on each peer's own machine, or spread across several peers. Other schemes exist, but the document says this one is the most useful and that labels like first and second generation only cause confusion.

sections.title: Applications Built with Peer-to-Peer Systems
sections.content:
Applications built this way fall into four domains: content distribution, distributed computing, collaboration and platforms.

Content distribution is what most people think of when they hear peer-to-peer, and they tend to think of illegal file sharing. The document argues that these systems are not intrinsically illegal: they are one of several means of storing and distributing content on the Internet, alongside HTTP and FTP servers, and it would be wrong to call HTTP illegal because some users upload material they may not distribute. Legitimate uses include the distribution of pre-recorded television programmes, Linux distributions, game updates and live television by parties authorised to distribute that content.

The main advantage of peer-to-peer content distribution is scalability. The peer holding the original content distributes it to a fraction of the peers interested in it, and those peers in turn distribute it to others, so the capacity of the system is not limited by the processing capacity and bandwidth of the peer with the original content. Peers can distribute the whole content, pieces of it, or combinations of pieces. There is generally no requirement for a peer distributing content to be able to access it, since the content may be encrypted so that peers without the decryption key are distributors but not consumers. The peer selection process shapes the character of the system, and the parties involved want different things: users want peers with the content, high bandwidth, high capacity and low latency; the operator of a content delivery network wants peers to connect first to those holding the rarest pieces, for reliability; and network operators prefer transfers to stay inside their own network so their peering and transit arrangements are not affected. Sometimes all of these can be met at once, and sometimes the system has to settle for acceptable trade-offs.

In distributed computing, each task is divided into independent subtasks that can be completed in parallel and delivered to a peer, which completes it with its own resources and returns the result; when all the subtasks are done their results are combined to give the result of the original task. Peers in such systems are typically spread geographically and joined by wide-area networks, unlike a cluster, where nodes are physically close and can be tightly integrated. The advantage is that a number of ordinary computers can deliver the performance of a much more powerful and usually more expensive computer. At present, though, it only applies to tasks that divide into independent subtasks that can run in parallel; other tasks are better done by one powerful computer. Most systems whose focus is distributed computing do not fully comply with the definition, because service requests come from a central node and most nodes never make requests, so Grid computing and SETI at home cannot strictly be considered peer-to-peer for that reason, and neither can MapReduce. Peer-to-peer botnets, despite the name, are in the same position, since the requests, such as generating spam or launching distributed denial-of-service attacks, usually come from one or a few central nodes; the Storm botnet is an example that propagates over a distributed hash table overlay and also uses a distributed command and control channel, which makes it harder to combat than botnets with centralised channels.

Collaboration applications include voice over IP and instant messaging, and include standard-based systems such as P2PSIP as well as proprietary ones. They typically provide rendezvous, network address translation traversal and a set of media-related functions such as mixing or transcoding, some of which are a form of distributed computing. Peer-to-peer rendezvous is especially useful where there is no infrastructure: a group with no internet connectivity setting up an ad hoc system to exchange documents, or a recovery team communicating in a disaster area.

Platforms provide functionality that applications built on top of them can use. JXTA is an example, offering peer discovery, grouping of peers and communication between peers, with the goal of becoming the preferred environment for application developers and taking advantage of the scalability of peer-to-peer systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists four kinds of use: sharing files, sharing computing work, talking to each other, and providing a platform for other applications. It stresses that file sharing is not illegal by itself, and that the same technology is used for television, Linux distributions and live TV.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Guidance
sections.content:
When deciding whether to use a peer-to-peer architecture, the general characteristics of such systems should be evaluated against the application's requirements. No definitive rule can be given, and the document provides a set of trade-offs to consider along with guidance on which kinds of requirement a peer-to-peer architecture meets better. Operational requirements have to be analysed case by case.

Peer-to-peer systems are a good option when there is no existing infrastructure and deploying it is difficult, so ad hoc systems are usually good candidates, and disaster areas where the infrastructure has been destroyed can benefit. Scalability is one of the main features: the system uses the processing and storage capacity of all its peers, so an increase in load is handled by peers using more of their capacity, and adding peers generally adds capacity as well as load, with no need to update central servers to deal with more users. Adaptive systems tune themselves as the number of peers or the churn rate changes, though maintaining a running distributed hash table currently takes nontrivial operational effort.

Robustness and reliability matter in many systems, and peers in a peer-to-peer system are not generally expected to be highly available, though a more expensive system of highly available peers is possible. These systems are designed to cope with peers leaving ungracefully, using data replication and redundant routing table entries so that data stored by a peer that crashes is not lost and can still be found.

Performance against a server-based system depends on many factors, and the type of task is one of the most important. If a task divides into independent subtasks that can run in parallel, a system of ordinary computers may beat even a supercomputer; for database queries, a well-dimensioned centralised database may be faster than a distributed hash table. Performance can also be hurt by a lack of cooperation between peers, so incentives matter to reduce the number of free riders. Scalability, robustness and performance trade against each other and can be influenced by configuration: a system where each peer stores everything would be robust and fast but neither efficient nor scalable, and storing only a part of the information increases efficiency and scalability at the expense of robustness and speed.

Energy consumption is another property. The overall consumption of a client-server system is generally lower than that of a peer-to-peer system offering the same service, but peer-to-peer avoids central server farms that can concentrate energy use in one place, and nodes that must run all the time anyway can be used in a peer-to-peer way. Using battery-powered devices as peers is harder, because a peer typically uses more energy than a client that can sleep more often.

The most important factor is often cost, both capital and operating. If updating a server to handle more load is inexpensive, a server-based architecture may be best; if a highly available server is expensive, a peer-to-peer system may be the better choice. In most scenarios there are no easy rules that say when to use which architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Peer-to-peer is the right answer when there is no infrastructure to build on, when the work can be split into pieces that run in parallel, and when a highly available server would be too expensive. It is the wrong answer when a central database answers queries faster, or when the users need a service to be up all the time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is important when choosing an architecture, and the first issue is how far the nodes in the system can be trusted. If all of them are fully trusted and under the full control of the operator, a peer-to-peer architecture can achieve a high level of security. If nodes are not fully trusted and can be expected to behave maliciously, providing an acceptable level of security becomes significantly harder than in a non-peer-to-peer environment, because of the distributed ownership and the lack of centralised control and global knowledge. The level of security a peer-to-peer system provides largely depends on the proportion of its nodes that behave maliciously, and with a large number of malicious nodes an acceptable level can easily become impossible to provide.

Peer-to-peer systems can also be used by attackers to harvest IP addresses in use. Attackers can passively obtain valid addresses of potential victims without active scanning, because a peer is typically connected to several others, and the attack is much more efficient than scanning when the address space is large and sparsely populated, as the current IPv6 address space is. There is often a high correlation between a particular application and a particular operating system, so harvested addresses can be useful for attacks on a specific operating system. On the other hand, central elements in centralised architectures are obvious targets, and peer-to-peer systems minimise the number of central elements, so they are more resilient against attacks aimed at a few elements.

Threats specific to peer-to-peer systems focus on data storage and routing. Messages between two peers generally traverse intermediate peers that route them, and those peers can launch on-path attacks they could not launch if they were not on the path. An attacker can choose a logical location in the overlay to launch such attacks against a particular victim, which is the Sybil attack; it can be mitigated by controlling how peers obtain their identifiers, for example through a central authority. A trivial passive attack is to read the contents of routed messages, and encrypting the parts not needed for routing is the obvious defence. An attacker can also forge a message and claim another peer created it, taking a legitimate message and modifying it, and peer and message authentication techniques avoid this. Against storage, an attacker may try to store too much data, mitigated by an enforceable quota system, or perform unauthorised operations on data objects, avoided by peer authorisation with peer authentication, or return forged or stale data objects, avoided by data object authentication and the use of lifetimes. Peer-to-peer-specific storage attacks include refusing to store an object or claiming an object does not exist when another peer created it; replication and multiple parallel searches mitigate these denial-of-service attacks. Against routing, an attacker may modify the routing of the system to mount on-path attacks, using forged routing maintenance messages, which is the Eclipse attack, mitigated by enforcing structural constraints or node degree bounds. Denial-of-service attacks can also be launched by modifying, dropping or forging routing maintenance messages, helped against by having nodes get routing tables from multiple peers, or by creating churn, leaving and joining the overlay rapidly, which can be limited by capping churn per node.
sections.plainLanguage: Security in these systems rests on trusting the nodes. When some nodes will lie, the peer that handles a message can read it or lie about the data it holds. The document lists the defences: authenticate peers and messages, encrypt what the routers do not need, replicate data, and limit how often a node can join and leave.

cells: Resolvers request service but do not provide it
User agents share resources only for their own sessions
User agents store each other's contact information in an overlay
Endpoints download pieces from and upload pieces to each other

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO INDEX THE DATA

cells: A central server keeps references to the data in all peers
Each peer keeps references only to its own data
References to data reside at several nodes

viz.caption: THE FUNCTIONS A PEER-TO-PEER SYSTEM PROVIDES

items.title: Enrollment
items.text: Authenticates and authorizes nodes joining the system.

items.title: Peer discovery
items.text: Lets a node find peers already in the system so it can connect.

items.title: Data indexing
items.text: Indexes the data stored in the system.

items.title: Data storage
items.text: Stores and retrieves data from the system.

items.title: Computation
items.text: Performs the computing the service needs, such as data processing.

items.title: Message transport
items.text: Exchanges messages between peers, directly or through a server or overlay.
